title: The minor rules
hookLine: the Buddha allowed minor rules to be dropped, but no one asked which; the elders kept them all
last: THE BINDING OF AN UNWRITTEN BOOK.

cards: Which rules are minor? It sounds like a small question. In the account of the Buddha's last days, he tells Ananda that after he is gone, the community may, if it wishes, set aside the lesser and minor rules.
It's a generous permission, a teacher loosening his grip and trusting his students. But it comes with a gap in it, and at the first council, the gap opens.

teach.b: At the council, Ananda tells the elders what the Buddha said: the minor rules may be dropped. The elders ask the obvious thing. Which ones?
Did you ask him? Ananda says no. He didn't ask.
The Vinaya lets us hear the elders trying. Some say every rule except the gravest ones is minor.

teach.h: SOME DRAW THE LINE HERE, SOME THERE.
teach.b: Others draw the line a little higher, then higher again. Each answer is reasonable. None of them settles it, because the one person who could settle it is gone.

Then Mahakassapa turns the question around. Lay people know which things are proper for monks, he says. If we start dropping rules now, they'll say the teacher's rules lasted only as long as the teacher, like smoke.
So let us not add rules the Buddha didn't make, and not take away rules he did make. The elders agree. They kept them all.
It cost Ananda something. After the council, the elders name several things he did wrong, and failing to ask which rules were minor is one of them.

Ananda says he didn't see it as a fault, but out of trust in the elders he acknowledges it. Some readers hear the elders being hard on him. Others hear the community choosing steadiness over its own best guess.
Either way, the council kept the whole set of rules, and in the Theravada telling, that is why the small rules are still kept alongside the great ones.

how: Theravada monks keep the full code of monastic rules, minor ones included, and recite it together at regular gatherings of the community.

games.why: Mahakassapa proposes keeping them all, so no one could say the rules lasted only as long as the teacher. the elders agree.

practice: Choose one small rule you already live by, or used to: closing the cupboard, answering a message the same day.
Decide to keep it fully today, not because it's important but because you said you would, and picture the moment it will come up.

wordCard.voice: Mahakassapa. He argued that no rule should be added or dropped, since the one person who could say which were minor was gone. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the lesser and minor, the words used for the rules the Buddha said could be set aside.

carryVoice: Your line: they kept them all. Not add, not take away. Day eight hundred fifty-three, done.
